name: Timeline for Repainting a High-Use Kitchen From Prep to Full Cure

step.name: Step 1: Prep the room and protect kitchen surfaces
step.text: Clear countertops, empty open shelving, and mask off cabinets, backsplashes, and appliances with plastic sheeting and painters tape. Cover flooring completely to keep dust, cleaning runoff, and paint splatters off hardwood or tile.

step.name: Step 2: Wash away accumulated grease and cooking residue
step.text: Scrub every wall and ceiling surface with a dedicated degreaser, focusing heavily on areas near the stove and range hood. Rinse thoroughly with clean water and let walls dry completely, as paint cannot bond to greasy films.

step.name: Step 3: Repair wall imperfections and smooth out glossy trim
step.text: Fill nail holes, patch gouges with joint compound, and lightly scuff-sand glossy existing enamel to create mechanical adhesion. Vacuum away sanding dust completely before wiping down walls with a clean microfiber cloth.

step.name: Step 4: Prime patched areas and difficult stains
step.text: Roll a high-quality stain-blocking primer over all compound patches, raw drywall, and stubborn cooking stains. Priming seals the surface evenly so finish coats do not flash or show patchy sheen variations across the wall.

step.name: Step 5: Apply the first coat of durable kitchen enamel
step.text: Cut in along the ceiling line and trim, then roll the primary coat using a washable satin, eggshell, or semi-gloss finish paint. Maintain a wet edge across each wall section to eliminate roller marks and lap lines.

step.name: Step 6: Allow proper recoat drying time
step.text: Let the first coat dry undisturbed for four to six hours depending on local indoor humidity and air movement. Rushing the second coat before the base layer dries can pull the fresh paint film and create surface texture flaws.

step.name: Step 7: Apply the final coat and protect while curing
step.text: Apply the second coat for rich color depth and complete coverage, then leave the space well-ventilated without heavy cooking for several days. Full cure takes time, so avoiding grease splatter and steam early on ensures a lasting finish.
